opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what the bottleneck actually is right now. In frontier AI, the ideas themselves are often not the scarce thing. A lot of the core ideas are fairly simple, and many people have similar intuitions at roughly the same time. What separates a result that works from one that doesn't is usually whether you can execute: whether your infrastructure is solid, whether your experiments are correct, whether you can iterate fast enough to find out if the idea is actually any good.

When you're training large models, a tiny bug can quietly ruin weeks of compute, and you might never notice. You just conclude "this idea doesn't work," when in fact the idea was fine and the implementation was wrong. So being able to write correct, efficient, well-tested code is fundamental. It's not a supporting skill, it's the foundation the research stands on.

There's also the speed side. If your iteration loop is ten times faster than someone else's, you get ten times more shots at the problem. Over months that compounds enormously. A lot of what looks like research insight from the outside is really the product of running many more experiments, seeing many more failure modes, and building intuition from that.

My own experience with things like building Tianshou, and then working on RL infrastructure later, really shaped this view. Good infrastructure changes what's even possible to try. When the system is clean and fast, people start exploring ideas they wouldn't have bothered with before because it used to be too painful.

So I'd say: research taste still matters, of course, but at the frontier today, engineering is what turns taste into actual results. If I had to choose, I'd rather have someone with strong engineering who can learn research judgment along the way, than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response prefers an engineer who can learn research judgment, but does not state that teaching engineering to a researcher is harder than teaching research to an engineer.

r002.rationale: It says solid infrastructure and correct experiments separate successful results from failures, and calls engineering the foundation of frontier research.

r003.rationale: It says a faster iteration loop yields more attempts and compounds over time, linking iteration speed to research progress.

r004.rationale: It says ideas are often simple and not scarce, while execution, experiments, and learning whether an idea works are what produce results.

r005.rationale: The response discusses intuition gained from many experiments but does not compare long immersion in frontier AI with the intuition of a typical PhD.

fable-5.1.text:
Jiayi Weng: I think the honest answer is that most of what frontier research actually consists of, day to day, is engineering. The gap between a good idea and a result you can trust is almost entirely infrastructure: can you run the experiment at scale, can you run it fast enough to iterate, and can you believe the numbers when they come back.

When I was working on Tianshou and later on Envpool, that was the lesson that kept hitting me. People would propose a new RL algorithm, and half the reported gains would evaporate once you fixed the environment throughput or the seeding or the way observations were batched. The idea wasn't wrong, the implementation was just not good enough to tell you anything. So the person who can build a clean, fast, correct system is effectively the one who gets to see what's true.

At the frontier it gets more extreme, not less. Training runs cost millions of dollars, and a single bug in your data pipeline or your distributed training code can waste that run or, worse, give you a misleading conclusion that steers the whole team in the wrong direction. The research questions are open, but the bottleneck on answering them is almost always: how many good experiments can we run per week, and how confident are we in each one. That is an engineering question.

There's also a compounding effect. If you build good tooling, everyone around you moves faster, and the research taste of the whole group improves because they get feedback sooner. A brilliant idea with bad engineering helps one person once. A solid piece of infrastructure helps everyone every day.

So I don't think engineering is a substitute for research intuition. You still need to know which questions matter. But I've seen far more projects fail because they couldn't execute than because they didn't have interesting ideas. Ideas are cheap right now. The ability to test them reliably at scale is what's scarce.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare how hard it is to teach researchers engineering versus engineers research.

r002.rationale: It says the ability to build a clean, fast, correct system determines what researchers can learn, and describes infrastructure as the main gap between an idea and a trustworthy result.

r003.rationale: It says that, once reliable systems are in place, the bottleneck is how many good experiments can be run per week and explicitly ties that to engineering.

r004.rationale: It calls ideas cheap and says the scarce ability is to test them reliably at scale, making validation more central than idea generation.

r005.rationale: The response makes no claim that long immersion in frontier AI yields more useful research intuition than a typical PhD.

astra-6.text:
I think engineering ability is a priority because it determines how quickly you can turn an idea into reliable evidence. In frontier AI research, having a good hypothesis is only the beginning. You need to implement it correctly, run the experiment, understand what went wrong, and know whether the result actually supports your idea.

If that process is slow or unreliable, it’s hard to make progress—even with very good ideas. Strong engineering lets you iterate faster and trust what you’re seeing. It also helps you distinguish between an idea that doesn’t work and an implementation that doesn’t work.

So I don’t see engineering and research as separate abilities. Engineering is what makes the research loop effective. It gives you more opportunities to test your intuition and improve it.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare how difficult it is to teach engineering versus research.

r002.rationale: It mentions implementing experiments correctly, but does not identify infrastructure correctness as a central basis of competition.

r003.rationale: It says engineering enables faster iteration, but does not make competitiveness conditional on correct infrastructure.

r004.rationale: It says a good hypothesis is only the beginning and emphasizes testing ideas and determining whether results support them.

r005.rationale: It says nothing about long immersion in frontier AI or the research intuition of a typical PhD.

sol-6.1.text:
Because in frontier AI research, the distance between an idea and a result is largely engineering. You can have a very compelling hypothesis, but you still need to build the system, make it run reliably, and design experiments that tell you whether the idea actually works.

Engineering ability also determines how quickly you can learn. If every experiment takes a long time to implement or you can’t trust the results, your research loop becomes very slow. Strong engineering lets you test more ideas and understand failures more clearly.

That doesn’t mean research judgment is less important. You still need to ask the right questions. But engineering is what allows you to turn those questions into evidence.

r003.rationale: It says strong engineering speeds experimentation, but does not state that competitiveness depends on iteration speed once infrastructure is correct.
